title: Cross stitch
subtitle: Two diagonal stitches crossed to make an X
excerpt: Cross stitch forms a small X by working one diagonal stitch and then crossing it with a second. It is worked both as a surface stitch over a drawn or transferred shape on plain-weave fabric, and counted over threads on Aida or evenweave.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), cross stitch entry.

content.text: Cross stitch is worked over a drawn shape on plain-weave fabric or counted over a set number of threads on Aida or evenweave. Each stitch is a small X made from two diagonal stitches. For a neat result, every top diagonal must lie in the same direction across the whole piece.

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 9 (tapestry needle for counted work)

content.text: Secure the thread on the back with a knot or two tiny stitches. Bring the needle up at A (bottom-left of the cross).
Insert the needle at B (top-right), completing the first diagonal. Bring it up at C (bottom-right).
Insert the needle at D (top-left) to complete the cross. The second diagonal now lies over the first.

To work a row of crosses quickly, stitch all the lower diagonals (A to B) along the row from left to right, then return right to left, adding the upper diagonals (C to D). Keep the crossing direction consistent throughout.

items.symptom: Top diagonals face in different directions
items.cause: The crossing direction was not kept consistent throughout the work.
items.fix: Choose one direction for the top stitch at the start and stick to it. A light pencil note beside the hoop helps.

items.symptom: The crosses look uneven or lumpy
items.cause: The four corner points are not forming a true square or rectangle.
items.fix: Mark the corners of each cross before stitching, or count threads carefully on evenweave. Equal arm lengths give a tidy X.
